CHAPTER 4.1 · LEARNING AREA 4

CHAPTER 4.1 · LEARNING AREA 4 · MARCH · APRIL

Rectangles

How much carpet does your room need? How long will the fence round the garden be? How many football pitches fit on the school grounds? For all of this you have to work out the area and perimeter of rectangles. You get to know the units of area from the square millimetre to the square kilometre and calculate figures that are made up of rectangles.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • compare areas by covering them with unit squares
  • derive and use the formulae for the area and perimeter of a rectangle
  • know units of area and convert between them
  • calculate composite figures by splitting them up and completing them

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Area and perimeter

If you cover the exercise book and the book with squares of the same size, you can count. Whoever needs more squares has the bigger area. With 24 m of fence there are the rectangles $1 \times 11$, $2 \times 10$, $3 \times 9$, $4 \times 8$, $5 \times 7$ and $6 \times 6$. The areas are 11, 20, 27, 32, 35 and 36 m². So the same perimeter does not mean the same area by a long way!

The area tells you how much space a figure covers. You measure it with unit squares: 1 cm² is a square with a side length of 1 cm. The perimeter is the length of the edge, once all the way round.

KEY POINT · RECTANGLE AND SQUARE

A rectangle with the side lengths $a$ and $b$ has

the area $A = a \cdot b$   and the perimeter $u = 2 \cdot a + 2 \cdot b$.

A square with the side length $a$ has $A = a \cdot a = a^2$ and $u = 4 \cdot a$.

Both sides must be given in the same unit.

Why times? A rectangle of 6 cm by 4 cm has 4 rows of 6 square centimetres each, so $4 \cdot 6 = 24$ cm².

Mixing up area and perimeter? Areas have units with “squared” (cm²), the perimeter is a length (cm).

INTERACTIVE · A RECTANGLE MADE OF SQUARES
EXAMPLE 1 · CARPET

A room is 4.5 m long and 3 m wide. How much carpet do you need? How long does the skirting board have to be if the door is 1 m wide?

$A = 4.5 \text{ m} \cdot 3 \text{ m} = 13.5 \text{ m}^2$. $u = 2 \cdot 4.5 \text{ m} + 2 \cdot 3 \text{ m} = 15 \text{ m}$, without the door 14 m.

13.5 m² of carpet, 14 m of skirting board

EXAMPLE 2 · BACKWARDS

A rectangle is 8 cm long and has an area of 40 cm². How wide is it? What is its perimeter?

$b = 40 \div 8 = 5$ cm. $u = 2 \cdot 8 + 2 \cdot 5 = 26$ cm.

5 cm wide, perimeter 26 cm

EXERCISES

Calculate the area and perimeter: a) $a = 7$ cm, $b = 3$ cm   b) $a = 12$ m, $b = 9$ m   c) square with $a = 15$ mm

a) 21 cm², 20 cm   b) 108 m², 42 m   c) 225 mm², 60 mm

Measure a page of your exercise book, your desk and a mobile phone. Calculate the area and perimeter of each.

For example an A4 sheet: 29.7 cm by 21 cm, so about 624 cm² and a perimeter of 101.4 cm.

A square has a perimeter of 36 cm. What is its area?

Side $36 \div 4 = 9$ cm, area $81$ cm².

Draw three different rectangles with an area of 24 cm². Which has the smallest perimeter?

For example $1 \times 24$ (u = 50 cm), $2 \times 12$ (28 cm), $3 \times 8$ (22 cm), $4 \times 6$ (20 cm). The perimeter is smallest for $4 \times 6$, the “most square” rectangle.

If you double both sides of a rectangle, what happens to the perimeter and what happens to the area? Try it out in the widget and explain.

The perimeter doubles, the area becomes four times as big: $2a \cdot 2b = 4 \cdot a \cdot b$. You can put the big rectangle together from four small ones.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Units of area and composite figures

About four people can stand on a square metre of newspaper. A square metre is 10 dm long and 10 dm wide, so $10 \cdot 10 = 100$ dm². That is why the conversion factor for areas is not 10 but 100.

KEY POINT · UNITS OF AREA

1 cm² = 100 mm² · 1 dm² = 100 cm² · 1 m² = 100 dm² · 1 a = 100 m² · 1 ha = 100 a · 1 km² = 100 ha

An are (a) is a square of 10 m by 10 m, a hectare (ha) a square of 100 m by 100 m.

You calculate composite figures by splitting them up into rectangles or by completing them to make a big rectangle from which you take away a piece.

Ares and hectares are used for plots of land, fields and forests. A football pitch is roughly 0.7 ha.

INTERACTIVE · SPLITTING UP OR COMPLETING
INTERACTIVE · THE UNIT STAIRCASE FOR AREAS
EXAMPLE 3 · CONVERTING

a) 3 m² into dm²   b) 450 cm² into dm²   c) 2.5 ha into m²

a) $3 \cdot 100 = 300$ dm²   b) $450 \div 100 = 4.5$ dm²   c) $2.5 \cdot 100 \cdot 100 = 25{,}000$ m²

EXAMPLE 4 · L-SHAPED ROOM

A room has the shape of a rectangle of 6 m by 5 m with a corner of 2 m by 2 m missing. How big is it?

Completing: $6 \cdot 5 - 2 \cdot 2 = 30 - 4 = 26$ m². Splitting up gives the same: $4 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 3 = 20 + 6$.

26 m²

EXERCISES

Convert: a) 5 dm² into cm²   b) 700 mm² into cm²   c) 4 a into m²   d) 30,000 m² into ha   e) 2 km² into ha

a) 500 cm²   b) 7 cm²   c) 400 m²   d) 3 ha   e) 200 ha

Which unit fits? The area a) of a postage stamp   b) of a classroom   c) of a farm   d) of Saxony

a) cm² or mm²   b) m²   c) ha   d) km² (Saxony has about 18,450 km²)

Draw a T made of two rectangles: at the top 8 cm by 2 cm, below it in the middle 2 cm by 5 cm. Calculate the area and perimeter.

Area $16 + 10 = 26$ cm². Perimeter: at the top $8 + 2 + 2$, plus the two steps of 3 cm each, the two long sides of 5 cm each and 2 cm at the bottom: $8 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 5 + 2 = 30$ cm.

A garden is 25 m long and 16 m wide. In it there is a garden shed of 4 m by 3 m. The rest becomes lawn. How much lawn is that in m² and in a?

$400 - 12 = 388$ m² = 3.88 a

A picture frame measures 30 cm by 40 cm on the outside, and the frame is 5 cm wide all the way round. How big is the area of the frame itself?

Inside there are $20 \cdot 30 = 600$ cm² left. Frame: $1200 - 600 = 600$ cm².

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A school playground is 60 m long and 35 m wide. How big is it in m², in a and in ha?

2,100 m² = 21 a = 0.21 ha

Connecting with chapter 3.1: Draw the rectangle A(1, 1), B(9, 1), C(9, 6), D(1, 6) with 1 cm per unit. Calculate the area and perimeter. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

8 cm by 5 cm: 40 cm², perimeter 26 cm. Two lines of symmetry, $x = 5$ and $y = 3.5$.

How many squares can you see on a chessboard with 8 by 8 squares if you also count the big squares made of several squares?

First count the 1×1 squares, then the 2×2 squares, and so on.

$64 + 49 + 36 + 25 + 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 204$ squares.

EXCURSIONEVERYDAY LIFE

The football pitch as a measure

On the news you often hear: “The forest fire was as big as 300 football pitches.” But how big is a football pitch actually? The Laws of the Game do not fix a size. For international matches it must be between 100 m and 110 m long and between 64 m and 75 m wide. For stadiums FIFA recommends 105 m by 68 m.

That is $105 \cdot 68 = 7{,}140$ m², so a good 71 ares or about 0.7 hectares. So a square kilometre is about as big as 140 football pitches.

Work it out yourself: How many football pitches would your school grounds be? And how many football pitches would fit on the area of Dresden, about 328 km²?

Sources: IFAB: Laws of the Game, Law 1 “The Field of Play”. FIFA: Football Stadiums. Technical Recommendations and Requirements, section on pitch dimensions.

Solution for Dresden: 328 km² = 32,800 ha, divided by 0.714 ha that makes roughly 46,000 football pitches.

6 cm, 4 cm: 24 cm²

PERIMETER

6 cm, 4 cm: 20 cm

UNITS OF AREA

conversion factor 100: mm², cm², dm², m², a, ha, km²

2.5 ha = 25,000 m²

COMPOSITE FIGURES
